detailed_rationale:
Garware Hi-Tech Films manufactures specialty plastic films across several segments: paint-protection films (PPF, a fast-growing premium auto-accessory category), sun-control window films, architectural films, and legacy BOPET/polyester films (a globally oversupplied, largely commoditized category). Value-added products now account for approximately 87% of revenue, and the PPF segment specifically grew 25% YoY, with a second PPF production line and a new TPU extrusion line coming online through late 2025/2026 as capacity catalysts. Yet FY26 (Mar 2026) consolidated revenue growth was just 1% on a trailing-twelve-month basis (sales of Rs 2,120 crore, net profit Rs 338 crore) — despite the 87% specialty mix and 25% PPF growth, consolidated growth is essentially flat, which is best explained by continued weakness/price pressure in the legacy BOPET/polyester film business (a structural, industry-wide oversupply problem, not specific to Garware) largely offsetting genuine double-digit growth in the specialty segments.

The stock's price action is starkly disconnected from this reported growth: a roughly 96% three-year and 115% one-year share-price CAGR (per market data), consistent with the CSV's very strong stage-timing momentum score (95/100), against just 1% trailing revenue growth. The market is clearly pricing in management's own FY27 guidance of 20-25% CAGR once the new PPF and TPU lines ramp — a real, plausible catalyst, but one that has not yet shown up in delivered consolidated numbers, and the second PPF line (originally targeted to start by September 2025) running alongside a results print still showing only 1% TTM growth suggests either a slower-than-guided ramp or a BOPET drag larger than currently disclosed.

The balance sheet is a genuine positive (almost debt-free, borrowings down to Rs 16 crore from Rs 141 crore, ROCE around 18% on the latest live figures — better than the CSV's slightly stale 13% figure, used here per standard practice of preferring the better live number), but at a PE of roughly 48x on essentially flat consolidated earnings growth, this is a name where the price has run well ahead of the demonstrated numbers, making the valuation entirely dependent on the new capacity delivering the guided step-change in growth.
recommendation_rationale: Quant recommendation is Hold on both axes. The specialty-film growth story is real, but the large gap between the stock's price appreciation and the still-flat consolidated revenue growth is a genuine valuation risk that argues against reading anything more constructive into this name than Hold.
summary: Garware Hi-Tech Films makes specialty plastic films, including a fast-growing paint-protection-film business, but consolidated revenue growth is still nearly flat (1% trailing twelve months) as legacy commodity polyester-film weakness offsets the specialty growth. The stock has rallied over 100% in the past year on expectations that new capacity coming online will deliver a step-change in growth, a story that has not yet shown up in the numbers. At roughly 48x earnings on flat growth, we rate it a Hold with real valuation risk if the capacity ramp disappoints.
positive_para: The paint-protection-film business is a genuine, fast-growing, premium niche (25% YoY growth) riding rising auto-accessory premiumization, value-added products are now 87% of the portfolio, the balance sheet is almost debt-free, and two new production lines (PPF and TPU extrusion) coming online through 2026 offer real capacity-driven upside if they ramp as guided.
negative_para: Consolidated revenue growth has been essentially flat (1% TTM) despite the specialty-mix shift, most likely because legacy BOPET/polyester film weakness (a structural, industry-wide oversupply issue) is offsetting genuine PPF growth, and the stock's more-than-doubling over the past year has priced in management's 20-25% FY27 CAGR guidance well before that growth has shown up in delivered results — if the new capacity ramps more slowly than guided, or if BOPET weakness persists, the current ~48x multiple has substantial room to compress.
reverse_dcf_judgment: A ~48x multiple on a business with just 1% trailing consolidated revenue growth is priced almost entirely for a future step-change from new capacity that has not yet appeared in the numbers; this is a legitimate but unproven story, so a forward estimate should credit real capacity-driven upside without simply adopting management's 20-25% guidance at face value, given the demonstrated gap between that guidance and delivered results so far.
